patient.name: Margaret Doyle
patient.complaint: Carers report 4 days of 'diarrhoea' and soiling, and she is off her food
background: Hip osteoarthritis; co-codamol 30/500 started 3 weeks ago
Drinks little because she worries about getting to the toilet

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis/cause?' with an elderly, immobile patient on opioids, or a hidden secondary cause (hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, cancer); overflow diarrhoea is the classic twist.

points: Carers find **watery, foul-smelling** stool on her pads for 4 days.
Before that, no bowel opening for **9 days**.
Occasional hard pellets; lower abdomen 'feels full'.

steps.lead: Nine days without opening her bowels, then hard pellets: Margaret is **constipated**, whatever the carers call it.
Margaret has four causes at once: **codeine** (opioid), **amlodipine** (CCB), **immobility** and **dehydration**.

steps.q: Which of Margaret's medicines is the most likely culprit?
steps.r: The constipation started after **co-codamol** (codeine, an opioid). Amlodipine also slows motility but she has taken it for years.

steps.lead: Her abdomen is full with a **palpable stool burden** and mild tenderness; DRE finds **hard stool** packed in the rectum.

visual.title: Where Margaret's stool burden is felt
visual.caption: Indentable, non-tender masses along the left colon: stool, not tumour (it moves and indents).

steps.lead: Watery stool after days of nothing, plus hard pellets, in an elderly immobile woman: **overflow diarrhoea** from **faecal impaction**.

visual.title: Bristol stool chart
visual.label: Margaret: type 7 leaking past type 1
visual.caption: Type 7 on the pad with type 1 pellets: liquid stool is **leaking around** the impaction.

steps.text: Do not give **loperamide** for 'diarrhoea' in an immobile elderly patient. Overflow is treated as **impaction**.

steps.lead: If left, Margaret risks an **anal fissure** from passing hard stool and **dehydration**.
In a **neonate** who has not passed meconium by 48 hours, think **Hirschsprung's**, not simple constipation.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' where the answer is clinical diagnosis plus basic bloods (FBC, TSH, calcium, U&Es), or FIT/colonoscopy when red flags appear.

steps.q: What makes the diagnosis of constipation?
steps.r: Constipation is a **clinical diagnosis**. Imaging adds nothing unless obstruction or red flags are suspected.

steps.lead: Margaret's history and DRE are enough to diagnose her: no scan needed.

steps.title: Margaret's bloods
steps.text: Normal TSH and calcium; raised urea suggests she is dry.

steps.lead: These **basic bloods** look for secondary causes: TSH for **hypothyroidism**, calcium for **hypercalcaemia**, FBC for anaemia. Her U&Es show **dehydration**.

visual.title: Adjusted calcium
visual.label: Margaret 2.38
visual.caption: Normal, so hypercalcaemia is not driving her constipation.

steps.lead: Margaret has no weight loss, bleeding or anaemia. If she were **over 50 with microcytic anaemia**, a **FIT** would be next.

steps.text: Red flags (weight loss, rectal bleeding, anaemia, change in habit in an older patient) switch you from laxatives to **colorectal investigation**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': lifestyle then bulk-forming, but impaction needs high-dose macrogol plus enema, and opioid constipation needs a stimulant plus osmotic.

steps.title: Laxative ladder
steps.caption: Impaction and opioid constipation skip steps.

steps.lead: For uncomplicated constipation the start is **fibre, fluids and activity**, then **ispaghula husk** with plenty of water.

steps.q: Margaret is impacted. What is the best initial treatment?
steps.r: **Impaction**: high-dose **macrogol** with an enema or suppository. Bulk-formers worsen impaction; loperamide treats the wrong problem.

steps.lead: Margaret gets **high-dose macrogol** and a phosphate **enema**; once cleared, **senna plus macrogol** while she needs codeine.
These second-line agents (**macrogol**, **senna**) and rectal measures keep her regular; carers set a toilet routine after breakfast.

visual.title: Margaret's bowel chart
visual.caption: Liquid overflow stops once the impaction clears; she settles at type 4.

steps.text: Bulk-forming laxatives are **not** for opioid-induced constipation or impaction: they add bulk to a bowel that is not moving.

points: Day 3: new **vomiting**, abdomen tight and distended.
No flatus since last night; severe crampy pain.

steps.lead: Vomiting, distension, severe pain and no flatus are **bowel obstruction** features: Margaret needs **urgent assessment**, not more laxatives.

points: Surgical review: abdominal X-ray shows faecal loading, no dilated loops.
Pain settles after an enema; flatus returns.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: how opioids or anticholinergics slow the gut, how each laxative class works, why overflow happens, or the embryology of Hirschsprung's.

steps.lead: Margaret's stool sat in a slow colon for days, so more and more **water was reabsorbed**, leaving it hard.
Codeine acts on **mu-opioid receptors** in the enteric nervous system: less motility, more fluid absorption.

o: Osmotically retains water in the lumen
steps.r: **Macrogol** is osmotic. Ispaghula is bulk-forming, senna stimulates enteric nerves, docusate is a softener.

steps.lead: Margaret's plan uses an **osmotic** (macrogol) to soften and a **stimulant** (senna) to push.

mcq.q: Which drug class commonly causes constipation?
mcq.r: **Opioids**, anticholinergics, CCBs and iron are the classics.

mcq.q: Watery, foul stool after days of constipation in an immobile elderly patient suggests?
Which metabolic cause of constipation should you test for?
Failure to pass meconium by 48 hours in a term neonate suggests?
Which basic bloods are taken in constipation?
When is a FIT indicated in a constipated patient?
Which laxative is first-line once lifestyle measures fail?
What is the management of faecal impaction?
mcq.r: Clear it with **macrogol** and a rectal agent.

mcq.q: Hirschsprung's disease results from failure of what?
mcq.r: **Neural crest** cells fail to reach the distal bowel: no ganglia.

prompts.q: What is constipation and what are its causes?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: always hunt for a drug or secondary cause.

points.p: Infrequent or difficult passage of hard stool, straining, incomplete evacuation
Low fibre, dehydration, immobility
Drugs: opioids, anticholinergics, CCBs, iron
points.why: Stem often hides a new drug.

points.p: Secondary: hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, colorectal cancer, Parkinson's
points.why: Why you check TSH and calcium.

prompts.q: What is overflow diarrhoea and who gets it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'diarrhoea' in an immobile elderly patient.

points.p: Watery, foul-smelling stool after long constipation, with hard stools
Reflects faecal impaction; treat as impaction
Elderly, immobile, palpable stool burden

prompts.q: What are the examination findings and complications of constipation?

points.p: Abdominal fullness, palpable stool, mild tenderness
DRE: hard stool, impaction or a rectal mass
points.why: A rectal mass is a red flag.

points.p: Complications: anal fissure, haemorrhoids, impaction, dehydration

prompts.q: How does Hirschsprung's disease present and how is it diagnosed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: neonate with no meconium.

points.p: Delayed meconium (>48 hours) in a term neonate
Intermittent pseudo-obstruction, no structural lesion
Rectal biopsy: absent ganglion cells

prompts.q: How is constipation investigated, and when do you go further?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: clinical first, red flags change everything.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis (gold standard)
FBC, TSH, calcium, U&Es
Red flags: colonoscopy or 2-week-wait
FIT if over 50 with microcytic anaemia

prompts.q: What is the stepwise management of simple constipation?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: lifestyle, bulk, then osmotic or stimulant.

points.p: Lifestyle: fibre, fluids, activity
Bulk-forming: ispaghula husk (with water)
Osmotic: macrogol or lactulose
Stimulant: senna or bisacodyl; rectal measures
points.why: Suppositories and enemas build a routine.

prompts.q: How do you treat faecal impaction, opioid constipation and constipation in children?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: special cases skip the bulk-former.

points.p: Impaction: high-dose macrogol plus enema or suppository
Opioid: docusate, or senna plus macrogol
Children: Movicol first, then lactulose, add senna

prompts.q: Which features mean this is no longer simple constipation and what do you do?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: no flatus is the stop sign.

points.p: Vomiting, distension, severe pain, no flatus
Urgent assessment, stop laxatives

prompts.q: How do opioids, anticholinergics and each laxative class work?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the receptor or the mechanism.

points.p: Opioids: mu receptors in enteric nervous system, less motility, more absorption
Anticholinergics: less parasympathetic drive, slower peristalsis
Bulk: absorbs water, more mass; osmotic: water into lumen
Stimulant: stimulates enteric nerves, more motility

prompts.q: Why do stools get hard, why does overflow happen, and what goes wrong in Hirschsprung's?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: transit time and water.

points.p: Slow transit lets the colon reabsorb more water
Liquid stool leaks around an impacted mass
Hirschsprung's: neural crest cells fail to migrate, aganglionic segment cannot relax

glossary.overflow diarrhoea: Liquid stool leaking around a hard impacted faecal mass, mimicking diarrhoea.
glossary.faecal impaction: A large, hard mass of stool stuck in the rectum or colon that cannot be passed.
glossary.Bristol stool chart: Seven-point scale of stool form: types 1 to 2 constipated, 6 to 7 liquid.
glossary.DRE: Digital rectal examination: a gloved finger in the rectum to feel stool, masses or tone.
glossary.stool burden: The amount of stool felt in the abdomen or seen on imaging.
glossary.anal fissure: A painful tear in the anal canal lining, usually posterior midline, from hard stool.
glossary.Hirschsprung's disease: Congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel causing functional obstruction.
glossary.meconium: A newborn's first, dark sticky stool, normally passed within 48 hours.
glossary.aganglionic: Lacking the nerve cell bodies (ganglia) that let the bowel wall relax.
glossary.ganglion cells: Enteric nerve cell bodies that coordinate bowel movement.
glossary.neural crest: Embryonic cells that migrate to form the gut's nerve plexuses, among other tissues.
glossary.pseudo-obstruction: Symptoms of bowel obstruction without a physical blockage.
glossary.anticholinergics: Drugs blocking acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, slowing the gut.
glossary.amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant with anticholinergic effects; causes constipation.
glossary.CCBs: Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine; can reduce intestinal motility.
glossary.amlodipine: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for hypertension; a drug cause of constipation.
glossary.opioids: Drugs such as codeine and morphine acting on opioid receptors; a common cause of constipation.
glossary.mu-opioid receptors: Opioid receptors in the gut wall that slow motility when activated.
glossary.enteric nervous system: The gut's own nerve network controlling motility and secretion.
glossary.hypercalcaemia: Raised blood calcium; causes constipation, thirst, polyuria and confusion.
glossary.hypothyroidism: Underactive thyroid; slows gut transit and causes constipation.
glossary.TSH: Thyroid stimulating hormone; raised in primary hypothyroidism.
glossary.FIT: Faecal immunochemical test for hidden blood in stool.
glossary.bulk-forming: Laxatives that absorb water to increase stool mass, such as ispaghula husk.
glossary.ispaghula husk: Bulk-forming laxative from plantago seeds; needs adequate fluid.
glossary.osmotic: Laxatives that draw and hold water in the bowel lumen.
glossary.Movicol: Brand of macrogol with electrolytes, taken as a drink.
glossary.lactulose: Osmotic sugar laxative, also fermented by gut bacteria.
glossary.stimulant laxative: Laxatives such as senna or bisacodyl that increase colonic motility via enteric nerves.
glossary.senna: Stimulant laxative, usually taken at night.
glossary.bisacodyl: Stimulant laxative available as tablets or suppository.
glossary.docusate sodium: Stool softener and weak stimulant, used for opioid-induced constipation.
glossary.enema: Fluid given into the rectum to soften and clear stool.
glossary.suppository: A solid medicine inserted into the rectum, where it dissolves.
glossary.tenesmus: Feeling of incomplete emptying or needing to go when the rectum is empty.
glossary.loperamide: Opioid antidiarrhoeal that does not cross into the brain; dangerous in impaction.
glossary.flatus: Gas passed from the bowel; absence suggests obstruction.

technique.stem: An 86 year old man in a nursing home has 3 days of frequent, foul-smelling watery stools and faecal soiling. Before this he had not opened his bowels for a week. He takes morphine for back pain. His abdomen is mildly distended with indentable masses in the left iliac fossa. Rectal examination shows hard stool.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about 'diarrhoea': ask what came before it.

clues: not opened his bowels for a week
steps.x: Opioid, immobile, a week of nothing, then liquid leak plus hard stool in the rectum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Overflow diarrhoea from **faecal impaction**.

elim: No antibiotics, fever or raised inflammatory markers; hard stool in the rectum.
Indentable masses are stool; no weight loss or bleeding.

steps.x: **E. Overflow diarrhoea.** Watery stool + hard rectal stool in the elderly = overflow; treat the impaction.

technique.stem: A 57 year old woman has 4 months of constipation, tiredness and feeling cold. She has gained 3 kg. There is no rectal bleeding. Abdominal and rectal examinations show soft stool only.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation: constipation is clinical, but bloods look for secondary causes.
Constipation with hypothyroid symptoms: basic bloods including **TSH**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The basic constipation screen: **FBC, TSH, calcium, U&Es**.

elim: No red flags (no bleeding, weight loss or anaemia).

steps.x: **D. FBC, TSH, calcium and U&Es.** Basic bloods first; colonoscopy only with red flags.

technique.stem: A 44 year old woman has 3 months of hard, infrequent stools. She is otherwise well and takes no medicines. Examination is normal. She has already increased her fibre and fluid intake and walks daily, without improvement.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?

steps.x: Initial drug treatment once lifestyle has failed.

clues: already increased her fibre and fluid intake
steps.x: Uncomplicated constipation, lifestyle tried: bulk-forming laxative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ispaghula husk**, with adequate water.

elim: Rectal stimulation is a later step.

steps.x: **C. Ispaghula husk.** Lifestyle → bulk-forming → osmotic/stimulant.

technique.stem: A 68 year old man starts regular codeine after a hip fracture. A week later he has hard stools and strains to pass them.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his constipation?
o: Calcium channel blockade in smooth muscle
Failure of neural crest cell migration
Mu-opioid receptor activation in the enteric nervous system

steps.x: Mechanism: link the drug to the gut.
Codeine is an opioid: mu receptors in the gut wall reduce motility and increase fluid absorption.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Mu-opioid receptor activation**.

elim: Metabolic cause; not linked to codeine.

steps.x: **E. Mu-opioid receptor activation in the enteric nervous system.** Opioids slow transit, so more water is absorbed.

practice.stem: An 88 year old woman with dementia has 5 days of faecal incontinence with brown liquid stool. Staff note she had no bowel opening for 10 days before this. Her temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 124/70 mmHg. The abdomen is soft with palpable stool. Rectal examination reveals a large hard faecal mass.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Liquid stool leaking around a hard impacted mass after 10 days of constipation is overflow; it is treated as impaction.

steps.x: Diagnosis of 'incontinence' in an elderly patient.
Liquid leak after prolonged constipation with an impacted rectum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Faecal impaction with overflow.**

elim: Afebrile, no antibiotics, and a hard faecal mass explains it.
Would give LIF pain and fever.
No vomiting, fever or contacts; preceded by 10 days of nothing.
The mass is faecal, not a fixed tumour.

steps.x: **C. Faecal impaction with overflow.** Treat as impaction, not diarrhoea.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has 2 months of constipation. His GP started a new antihypertensive 10 weeks ago. He takes no other new medicines. Examination is normal.
practice.q: Which antihypertensive is most likely responsible?
practice.e: Amlodipine (a calcium channel blocker) decreases intestinal motility and is a classic drug cause of constipation.

steps.x: Drug cause of constipation.
The antihypertensive that slows gut motility is a calcium channel blocker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Amlodipine.**

elim: Fatigue, cold peripheries and bradycardia; not a classic cause.

steps.x: **A. Amlodipine.** CCBs reduce intestinal motility.

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman has 6 months of constipation, weight gain, dry skin and low mood. Her pulse rate is 54 bpm and BP 136/88 mmHg. Ankle reflexes relax slowly.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her constipation?
practice.e: Raised TSH with low free T4, bradycardia and slow-relaxing reflexes makes hypothyroidism the secondary cause.

steps.x: Cause of constipation: look for systemic clues.
Bradycardia, weight gain, slow-relaxing reflexes, raised TSH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypothyroidism.**

elim: Weight gain, not loss; no bleeding.
Does not cause bradycardia, raised TSH or slow reflexes.

steps.x: **C. Hypothyroidism.** Always check TSH in constipation.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has 4 weeks of constipation, thirst, passing more urine and back pain. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. He looks dry.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his constipation?
practice.e: Constipation with polyuria, thirst and a calcium of 3.12 is hypercalcaemia, possibly from myeloma or bone metastases.

steps.x: Cause of constipation: thirst, polyuria, back pain.

clues: thirst, passing more urine and back pain
steps.x: 'Stones, bones, groans, moans': raised calcium.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hypercalcaemia.**

elim: Causes thirst and polyuria but not constipation or high calcium.
No leg weakness, sensory level or sphincter loss.

steps.x: **C. Hypercalcaemia.** Check calcium in every constipated patient.

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has 2 weeks of sharp, tearing anal pain on opening her bowels, lasting an hour afterwards, with bright red blood on the paper. She has been constipated with hard stools since starting iron tablets. Examination shows a small tear in the posterior midline of the anal canal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely complication of her constipation?
practice.e: Painful defecation with bright red blood and a posterior midline tear is an anal fissure, a complication of hard stool (from iron).

steps.x: Complication of constipation.

clues: sharp, tearing anal pain on opening her bowels
steps.x: Hard stool tearing the anoderm: posterior midline tear.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anal fissure.**

elim: Discharge from an external opening, usually after an abscess.
Constant throbbing pain with a hot, tender swelling.
A purple, tender lump at the anal margin.

steps.x: **A. Anal fissure.** Iron causes constipation; hard stool causes fissures.

practice.stem: A 3 day old boy born at term has not passed meconium. He has a distended abdomen and has started bilious vomiting. After rectal examination there is an explosive passage of stool and gas.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause?
practice.e: Delayed meconium beyond 48 hours in a term baby with explosive stool after rectal examination is Hirschsprung's; rectal biopsy confirms it.

steps.x: Cause of neonatal constipation.
No meconium by 48 hours plus explosive stool after DRE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hirschsprung's disease.**

elim: Vomiting in the first day with a double-bubble; meconium can pass.
Bilious vomiting but meconium passes; no explosive stool after DRE.
Non-bilious projectile vomiting at 2 to 8 weeks.

steps.x: **B. Hirschsprung's disease.** Confirm with rectal biopsy: no ganglion cells.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man has 3 months of constipation. He is tired. There is no rectal bleeding. Abdominal and rectal examinations are normal. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: A constipated patient over 50 with microcytic (iron-deficiency) anaemia needs a FIT; a positive result leads to colonoscopy.

steps.x: Next investigation: the FBC is abnormal.
Over 50 with **microcytic anaemia**: FIT, then colonoscopy if positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Shows faecal loading; does not look for cancer.
Coeliac usually causes diarrhoea; this is microcytic anaemia over 50.

steps.x: **C. Faecal immunochemical test.** Microcytic anaemia over 50 = look for colorectal cancer.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has 2 years of intermittent constipation. She is otherwise well, with no weight loss, bleeding or family history of bowel cancer. Abdominal examination and rectal examination are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Constipation is diagnosed clinically; with no red flags, imaging and endoscopy add nothing.

steps.x: How is constipation diagnosed?

clues: no weight loss, bleeding or family history
steps.x: Young, well, no red flags: history and examination confirm it.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clinical assessment.**

elim: Not needed; poor at assessing constipation.

steps.x: **C. Clinical assessment.** Constipation is a clinical diagnosis.

practice.stem: A 79 year old woman has palliative lung cancer and takes regular morphine. She has had hard stools every 4 days for 2 weeks. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 122/70 mmHg. Abdominal examination is soft and non-tender.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate laxative?
practice.e: Opioid-induced constipation is treated with a stimulant plus an osmotic (senna plus macrogol) or docusate; bulk-formers are avoided.

steps.x: Laxative for opioid-induced constipation.
Opioid constipation: stimulant plus osmotic (or docusate).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Senna and macrogol.**
**E. Senna and macrogol.** Avoid bulk-formers with opioids.

practice.stem: An 84 year old man in a care home has leakage of liquid stool after a week without opening his bowels. He is immobile. Rectal examination shows a large, hard faecal mass. His temperature is 36.7°C and BP 132/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Faecal impaction with overflow is cleared with high-dose macrogol plus an enema or suppository; loperamide is dangerous here.

steps.x: Initial management of overflow.
Faecal impaction: clear it with high-dose macrogol plus enema/suppository.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **High-dose macrogol and an enema.**

elim: Adds bulk to an impacted bowel.
No red flags; the mass is stool.

steps.x: **A. High-dose macrogol and an enema.** Overflow = impaction = macrogol + rectal agent.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man with chronic constipation takes senna. He now has 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and abdominal distension and has not passed flatus. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 104/64 mmHg. The abdomen is tympanic.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
practice.e: Vomiting, distension, colicky pain and no flatus suggest bowel obstruction, which needs urgent surgical assessment, not more laxatives.

steps.x: Next step: are these red flags?

clues: colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and abdominal distension
steps.x: Vomiting, distension, severe pain, no flatus: bowel obstruction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent surgical assessment.**

elim: Adds bulk to an obstructed bowel.
Too slow for an acute obstruction.

steps.x: **E. Urgent surgical assessment.** No flatus = stop laxatives, assess urgently.

practice.stem: A 52 year old woman with constipation is started on lactulose. She asks how it works.
practice.q: Which is the mechanism of action of lactulose?
o: Absorbs water to increase faecal mass
Draws water into the bowel lumen osmotically
practice.e: Lactulose and macrogol are osmotic laxatives: they draw water into the bowel lumen to soften stool.

steps.x: Mechanism of a laxative.
Lactulose is osmotic: it holds water in the lumen.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Osmotic water retention.**

elim: Opposite of what she needs; that causes constipation.

steps.x: **D. Draws water into the bowel lumen osmotically.** Osmotic: macrogol, lactulose.
